segments.t: We're still in the nineteen eighties, in the same communal flat. Last time, Vanya's father came home from Hungary with gum, markers and a toy car, and told him to share everything; little Arkady only watched. Now Arkady asks Vanya for a piece of gum, and soon the toy car goes missing. We'll hear it in Russian first; don't worry about catching every word.
Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
Let's go through it. The presents have been handed out, and Vanya is enjoying himself in front of Arkady.
'Well, four-eyes?' the expression for this is
It is built from which translates to glasses, a classic schoolyard taunt for a kid in specs. Then Vanya shows his empty hands.
'See, there's nothing left.' Literally, 'nothing didn't remain': in Russian, the Russian for nothing,
always pairs with the little word for not. Arkady knows that isn't true.
'But you've still got some.' Literally, 'at you there is more', with the tiny word
adding an insistent 'but you clearly do!'. Then he asks.
'Give me just one.' The action word
asks someone casually to hand something over, and the phrase
pleads for 'at least one'. The answer is short.
'No. That's mine.' the term meaning mine is
used when talking about things in general, even though his father told him to share. Arkady has one word for that.
'Greedy!' which translates to a greedy person is
It translates to what kids shout at anyone who won't share. Vanya doesn't care, and shows off his markers.
'See the markers? They're from Japan!' Literally, 'this is Japan' —
— which is how a boy boasts about foreign treasure. Suddenly something goes missing.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
'Hey, where's the toy car? Where's my toy car?' The describing word for my,
ends in an 'ah' sound to match which translates to toy car,
is the very same word for 'hold' Vanya's dad used when handing over gum, except
translates to 'hold him — grab him!'. Arkady struggles.
'Let go!' the term for let go is
It is a sharp one-word order to release someone. Vanya grins.
'Well, well, caught you, didn't we?' the Russian word
literally packs 'you got caught!' into a single action word. Arkady tries to explain.
'I was only looking!' The little word
translates to 'only' or 'just', and the action word
has a special ending for a boy speaker. Vanya gets a nasty idea.
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
'Look, how dirty our toilet is!' The action word
is built from the basic word for look, adding a special ending because Vanya is calling to all the kids at once. Then he adds something.
'It needs a wash!' the Russian word

translates to 'it's needed' or 'we ought to', and you'll hear it in almost every Russian conversation. What happens next is cruel: the boys dunk Arkady's head into the toilet bowl, and afterwards he makes a threat.
literally warns 'you will still regret it!'. Vanya just laughs at him.
is a scoffing two-word comeback that translates to 'oh really, come off it?'. Arkady answers.
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
'When I grow up, you'll be begging me to forgive you!' Where English uses a present action word in 'when I grow up', Russian literally says 'when I will grow up', using the phrase
Remember this line, because the whole series turns on it.
literally puts 'what' first and needs no little helper word like 'did' at all. Here's the whole scene once more.
Ну что, очкарик? Видишь, ничего не осталось.
У тебя же есть ещё. Дай хоть одну.
А где машинка? Где моя машинка?
Смотрите, какой у нас грязный унитаз!
Когда вырасту, ты будешь просить у меня прощения!
That's the promise little Arkady makes, and thirty years later he will get his chance. See you next time!
